source: Rasmussen & Jensen (1974) Mental procedures in real-life tasks: a case study of electronic trouble shooting
finding: Think-aloud study of skilled repairmen fixing real instruments at a nuclear research lab. They found fault finding is a search through a hierarchy (subsystem, stage, component) built from a few recurrent search routines.
numbers: 45 cases recorded, 30 analysed in detail. 6 technicians, 8 instrument types (22 analog, 8 digital systems). Each instrument had its own fault.
quote: The procedures found are organized as a search through a system which is viewed as a hierarchy of subunits.
limits: Small N, qualitative, no efficiency scores on purpose (to stop comparison between men). Verbalising may distort fast or parallel steps.
agent_relevance: Our agent should treat diagnosis as nested narrowing (system, subsystem, part), with a different test routine per level.

source: Rasmussen & Jensen (1974) Mental procedures in real-life tasks: a case study of electronic trouble shooting
finding: Three routines are named: topographic search (trace the signal and give each point a good/bad verdict), functional search (match a faulty feature of the response to the subsystem that makes it), and search by evaluation of the fault (reason from the faulty response to a cause and a location). The word 'symptomatic' is NOT in this paper; it comes later from Rasmussen 1981/1986.
numbers: Counts of routines in the 30 protocols: 31 functional, 82 topographic, 87 evaluations of fault mode, 75 check measurements.
limits: Terminology drifts: in 1974 'topographic' means scanning by position with good/bad checks; in Rasmussen's later reviews it means search against a model of normal operation. Cite the year when using the term.
agent_relevance: Name our test types by what they need: a normal-state reference (topographic), a symptom-to-part map (functional), or a causal model (evaluation).

source: Rasmussen & Jensen (1974) Mental procedures in real-life tasks: a case study of electronic trouble shooting
finding: Technicians prefer many cheap, independent good/bad checks over a few well-chosen measurements plus reasoning. Authors call this informationally wasteful but rational if the aim is to save time and mental load.
numbers: In the digital scaler example the design engineer used a few observations and complex reasoning; the technician scanned the faulty decade with a rapid stream of good/bad checks and then ohm-checked fewer than half a dozen resistors.
quote: Seen from the viewpoint of information economy, the procedures are inefficient, but ... very rational.
limits: Rationality claim is argued, not measured: no time or cost data were collected.
agent_relevance: Cost-weighted view: a cheap but redundant test can beat an optimal but expensive-to-plan test. Our agent should price thinking cost too, not only measurement count.

source: Rasmussen & Jensen (1974) Mental procedures in real-life tasks: a case study of electronic trouble shooting
finding: Where the search starts and how often it works. Functional search is mostly the opening move. About 70% of 82 topographic searches took their search field from a previous search or from a decision to repeat. Only about 40% of topographic searches succeeded and started a local search.
numbers: Of 31 functional searches nearly 70% were sent to the next field by the failed function alone. After an unsuccessful topographic search: 23% return to an earlier indication, 17% repeat the search, 10% take a break. Of 75 check measurements: 45% confirm a fault location, 30% confirm a 'what to look for' hypothesis, about 20% serve as individual points in an overall topographic search (split-half style).
limits: Percentages come from a single lab, 30 protocols, coded by the authors.
agent_relevance: Baseline rates for an agent: opening move is by function, most failures are met by repeating, so a repeat-detector is worth building.

source: Rasmussen & Jensen (1974) Mental procedures in real-life tasks: a case study of electronic trouble shooting
finding: Split-half appears only as a minor variant: for a cascade of subsystems the man picks check points between subsystems 'like the split half search', and checks were chosen where norm data are already known, not where information is highest.
numbers: About 20% of 75 check measurements served as individual points in an overall topographic search (the split-half case). No count of strict halving is given.
quote: The measuring points for good/bad checks are then selected individually between the sub systems (like the split half search).
limits: The paper does not test half-split against anything; it only notes it.
agent_relevance: Half-split is a trained rule, not the natural human strategy. Check placement was set by where a reference value exists; our agent needs a reference value for every test it chooses.

source: Rasmussen & Jensen (1974) Mental procedures in real-life tasks: a case study of electronic trouble shooting
finding: Fixation: when the routine fails, men repeat it with another parameter (DC voltage then AC, and back), then go back to an earlier search, rather than reason from how the specific system works. Suggesting a functional-reasoning approach did not change later records.
numbers: Topographic search failed to give a local search in more than one half of attempts. The suggestion to use functional reasoning gave no significant change in later records.
quote: In cases where they are unsuccessful, there seems to be a fixation, resulting in a tendency to rely on repetitions.
limits: Qualitative report; no counts for the suggestion test. A waste-tank level system with serious consequences did trigger careful advance reasoning.
agent_relevance: Direct support for guardrail G1 and the impasse trigger: after a failed routine, force a change of method (a different test class), not a repeat.

source: Rasmussen & Jensen (1974) Mental procedures in real-life tasks: a case study of electronic trouble shooting
finding: Information in an observation is dropped once a familiar search field is chosen ('point of no return'). Men judge each reading good or bad and discard the value; some hints show up only after a break.
numbers: Authors also note the men did not check whether a measuring point was informationally redundant.
quote: Although more information in the observation is clearly available ... the decision locks out the influence of such information.
limits: Interpretation by the authors; no experiment isolates the cause.
agent_relevance: An agent that keeps raw results in a ledger (code-held) avoids this loss; a model that summarises as it goes will behave like these men.

source: Burroughs (1979) An investigation of mental coding mechanisms and heuristics used in electronics troubleshooting (Univ. Oklahoma dissertation; includes a literature review)
finding: Describes the half-split rule as taught since Miller, Folley & Smith (1953): test input and output of a chain; if input is good and output bad, test the middle of the bad half; repeat. Steps needed are log2 N for N units in a chain.
numbers: 8-stage example needs 3 checks. For a divergent flow the rule differs: if any output is normal, suspect the stage at the divergence point.
limits: The log2 N claim holds for a single fault, a linear chain, equal test cost and reliable tests only.
agent_relevance: Half-split is the equal-cost, single-fault, uniform-prior special case; code can compute it exactly on a candidate list.

source: Burroughs (1979) An investigation of mental coding mechanisms and heuristics used in electronics troubleshooting (Univ. Oklahoma dissertation; includes a literature review)
finding: Direct count of strategy use by two expert TV repairmen over 40 trials. Not one trial used half-split, middle-to-trouble or output-to-input; one used input-to-output. Localisation was mostly done by 'anchoring and adjustment' from a hunch or signal flow.
numbers: 2 certified technicians x 20 trials = 40 trials. Fault-localisation stage actions: half split 0, middle-to-trouble 0, out-to-in 0, in-to-out 1, anchor and adjust 8, schematics 5, senses 4. First stage: use of senses in 40 of 40 trials, power to chassis 38/40.
quote: The more traditional approaches to localization (half split, input to output, etc.) were almost totally ignored by technicians in favor of anchoring and adjustment.
limits: Only 2 subjects, TV sets, observer coding by one researcher, so weak statistics; but the 0 of 40 is clear.
agent_relevance: Experts do not half-split in practice. Matches Rasmussen & Jensen: formal textbook strategies are not what skilled people do. The agent need not copy human practice; it can do better with code.

source: Burroughs (1979) An investigation of mental coding mechanisms and heuristics used in electronics troubleshooting (Univ. Oklahoma dissertation; includes a literature review)
finding: Report of the USC Bayesian model (BETS, Rigney et al. 1966-67): choose each next test by largest expected uncertainty reduction on a symptom-malfunction matrix. Trainees were far less efficient than the model.
numbers: 39 trainees on one circuit, six malfunctions each: about one third as efficient as BETS. Follow-up with 36 advanced trainees: better in time, steps and correct solutions; only a little over half behaved like Bayesian processors.
limits: Reported second-hand through Burroughs; Burroughs notes BETS did not separate skill groups (it was too insensitive) and judged it unrealistic for human memory limits.
agent_relevance: The information-gain rule beats humans by about 3x on test efficiency in this early study. It is the natural job for code, with the model supplying only the symptom-malfunction table.

source: Burroughs (1979) An investigation of mental coding mechanisms and heuristics used in electronics troubleshooting (Univ. Oklahoma dissertation; includes a literature review)
finding: Bryan & Schuster (1959) and Rigney et al. (1961) records of real fault finding: technicians often held enough information to isolate the fault but did not notice, and kept making redundant checks; most first replacements were wrong.
numbers: 422 records reviewed; 71% of first replacements were incorrect.
limits: Old field data (military electronics) and described second-hand.
agent_relevance: Search for evidence and reading the evidence are separate skills. Code should check after each test whether the candidate set is already a single item.

source: Burroughs (1979) An investigation of mental coding mechanisms and heuristics used in electronics troubleshooting (Univ. Oklahoma dissertation; includes a literature review)
finding: Evans & Smith (1953) saw perseveration: some technicians kept testing stages that earlier results already ruled out, mostly in the stage they knew least about.
numbers: 10 subjects observed, 5 common and 5 unique problems, paper simulation; a small share of subjects showed it (no exact share given).
limits: Preliminary study; funding was lost, so little else was reported.
agent_relevance: A candidate ledger in code that marks ruled-out parts blocks this failure directly.

source: Burroughs (1979) An investigation of mental coding mechanisms and heuristics used in electronics troubleshooting (Univ. Oklahoma dissertation; includes a literature review)
finding: Taught rule set (Miller et al. 1953 era): for unambiguous test results use half-split; for ambiguous results test another point as near as possible until the reading is unambiguous.
numbers: Rule given as part of an instructional strategy for the Isolation stage, after Symptom Pattern Completion and Localization.
limits: Rule set is prescriptive; the cited studies teach it, they do not prove it beats other orders.
agent_relevance: Gives our agent a fallback when a test is noisy: repeat nearby before trusting the verdict.

source: Simon & Kadane (1975) Optimal problem-solving search: all-or-none solutions
finding: Formal result for searching for ANY one goal when each site has a probability p and a cost c: the order that minimises expected cost is by descending ratio p/c (probability per cost). Proved by an exchange argument.
numbers: Expected cost V(ab)=V(a)+S(a)V(b), S(ab)=S(a)S(b); swapping neighbours a,b changes cost by S(prefix)[V(b)P(c)-V(c)P(b)]. Treasure example with Q sites.
limits: One goal, independent sites, tests whose failure leaves the rest unchanged. Does not cover splitting a candidate set by a test that gives information on many candidates at once. The scan text is OCR-garbled, so the ratio is read from the proof structure.
agent_relevance: This is the cost-weighted rule for 'check the likely and cheap part first'. Code can sort candidates by p/c.

source: Simon & Kadane (1975) Optimal problem-solving search: all-or-none solutions
finding: Extends to partially ordered search (slices that must be done top-down) by joining slices into indivisible blocs; an optimal strategy is a sequence of maximal blocs with p/c ratios falling.
numbers: Theorems 2.1-2.4 and Corollary 2.3.1 (proofs given). Third section handles several alternative goals.
limits: Precedence order must be known; unrealistic when access cost depends on previous tests (e.g. disassembly).
agent_relevance: Maps to troubleshooting where some checks need earlier steps (open the case first). Group a prerequisite and its test as one bloc and rank the bloc.

source: Simon & Kadane (1975) Optimal problem-solving search: all-or-none solutions
finding: Separates three search types: best-value, shortest-path and satisficing. Fault finding is satisficing: find the one fault and stop; needed information differs from best-value search.
numbers: Needle example: satisficing effort depends on density of good sites and not on haystack size.
limits: Conceptual framing; no empirical test in the paper.
agent_relevance: Our agent's stop rule is 'first confirmed fault', not 'best explanation of everything'; cost and ordering theory differs accordingly.

source: Venkatasubramanian et al. (2003) A review of process fault detection and diagnosis, Part II: qualitative models and search strategies
finding: Formal typology: topographic search uses a template of NORMAL operation and finds the fault as a mismatch located in the system; symptomatic search uses the abnormal observations as a template matched against known fault patterns. Attributed to Rasmussen (1986).
numbers: Topographic can be structural (follow information paths; keep bad paths, remove parts that also sit on good paths) or functional (check function of groups of parts down a hierarchy).
quote: Topographic searches perform malfunction analysis using a template of normal operation, whereas, symptomatic searches look for symptoms to direct the search to the fault location.
limits: Secondary review of chemical process diagnosis, not an experiment; the functional/structural split here differs a little from Rasmussen & Jensen's 1974 sense.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean split for the schema: normal-reference search handles novel and multiple faults; pattern match is cheap but needs a library of known faults.

source: Venkatasubramanian et al. (2003) A review of process fault detection and diagnosis, Part II: qualitative models and search strategies
finding: Stated trade-off: topographic search needs no model of faults, so is insensitive to novel and multiple faults, but returns a set of hypotheses and often poor resolution. Symptomatic search is economical but needs a reference pattern of the actual abnormal state and struggles with novel or multiple faults.
numbers: Qualitative claim from the review; no benchmark numbers.
limits: Review claim, not measured head to head.
agent_relevance: Use topographic search to narrow the region first, symptomatic matching to pick within it; match the stated strengths.

source: Venkatasubramanian et al. (2003) A review of process fault detection and diagnosis, Part II: qualitative models and search strategies
finding: Hypothesis-and-test (closed loop: generate a hypothesis, simulate its effects, compare to data) and open-loop (many reference models compared at once). Efficiency depends on how well hypotheses are generated; Peng & Reggia used probability to make the most likely hypotheses come first.
numbers: Parsimonious covering theory (prefer simple covers). Hypotheses can come from either topographic or symptomatic search.
limits: Descriptive; complexity grows with multiple faults.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis generation can stay with the model; ranking and testing by code (fits G5).

source: Feldman, Provan & van Gemund (2010) A model-based active testing approach to sequential diagnosis
finding: Formal framework for choosing the next test (active testing) in model-based diagnosis: greedy choice of the input setting that lowers the expected number of remaining minimal-cardinality diagnoses; compared with ATPG-based and probing baselines on ISCAS85/74XXX circuits.
numbers: Remaining diagnoses fall as a geometric decay with rate p; FractalATPG average p = 0.73 with goodness-of-fit R2 = 0.84. FractalG differs from exhaustive control search by 5.4% in decay rate on 74182 and is far faster; exhaustive times out above 20 controls.
limits: Combinational digital circuits only, simulated faults; greedy can be made arbitrarily bad by constructed models (authors say so).
agent_relevance: One-step greedy information gain is near enough optimal in tested circuits and costs little; use it for the agent's test selector.

source: Feldman, Provan & van Gemund (2010) A model-based active testing approach to sequential diagnosis
finding: Cites theory behind greedy test choice: Pattipati & Alexandridis (1990) show a one-step look-ahead gives the optimal average test-tree depth under unit test cost and equal fault priors; de Kleer, Raiman & Shirley (1992) find one-step look-ahead good in practice. Optimal test sequencing is infeasible at realistic size, and multiple-fault sequential diagnosis is super-exponential.
numbers: Optimal test sequencing is called NP-hard by the authors; multiple fault diagnosis is 2p-hard.
limits: Taken from the related-work text of this paper; the original Pattipati and de Kleer papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports using a cheap one-step rule instead of a deep planner; flag the unit-cost and equal-prior conditions where it is exactly optimal.

source: Feldman, Provan & van Gemund (2010) A model-based active testing approach to sequential diagnosis
finding: Exponential increase in the number of controllable inputs gives little extra decay: even turning a few inputs into controls gives near-optimal decrease in remaining diagnoses.
numbers: Table 10 average p versus control bits; running time of FractalG from 7.1 s (74182) to 2382 s (c6288).
limits: Compute cost is dominated by the expectation step; scale limits to circuits tested.
agent_relevance: Test menu does not need to be huge: a small, well-chosen set of probe actions is enough.

source: Gonzalez-Sanchez et al. (2011) Spectrum-based sequential diagnosis
finding: Sequential diagnosis for software: greedily pick the next test from a suite by entropy drop on Bayesian posterior over fault candidates, with approximate entropy. Handles multiple and intermittent faults at polynomial cost.
numbers: Test reduction up to 80% against random test order on Siemens suite programs and 3 Unix programs; each point averaged over 100 runs; fault density 10 faults/KLOC (prior 0.01).
limits: With real test outcomes gains shrink; on tcas and tot_info it was WORSE than random because intermittency was poorly estimated and ambiguity groups were large.
agent_relevance: Dynamic, outcome-based test choice beats fixed order, but only if the probability model is right; wrong probabilities can lose to random. The agent should audit its estimates.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts
finding: Uncertainty of Thoughts: LLM simulates answers to candidate questions and picks the one with best expected information gain. Tested on 20 Questions, medical diagnosis and a troubleshooting dialogue set (FloDial: 894 dialogues, 153 faults for car and laptop).
numbers: Average success-rate gain +38.1% over direct prompting across 5 datasets and 5 LLMs. Troubleshooting with GPT-4: success 43.7% to 67.3% with 7.8 mean questions; up to 20 turns.
limits: Answerer simulated by GPT-4; the authors call the troubleshooting benchmark simplified; questions are dialogue questions, not instrument measurements.
agent_relevance: Best direct LLM evidence that explicit information-gain question choice helps in fault-style dialogues. Still the model estimates probabilities, which breaks our G5 rule; do the counting in code.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM
finding: BED-LLM (ICLR 2026): choose each question by expected information gain computed from the LLM's own predictive distribution, with a filtering step on hypotheses. Beats prompt-only and a 'Split' baseline (choose the question that most evenly splits sampled hypotheses, i.e. half-split by sampling).
numbers: 20 Questions on Animals, Celebrities, Things (100 targets each): average +37.4 percentage points over direct prompting; success rate more than doubles in over half of setups and never decreases. Split is the previous best method and BED-LLM beats it across all problems and LLMs.
limits: Game setting, simulated answerer; Split assumes a deterministic likelihood, and BED-LLM shows pure-entropy choice wastes turns on noisy questions.
agent_relevance: The measured gap between half-split (Split) and full information-gain is a clean LLM-era version of the half-split vs cost-aware debate; use noise-aware gain, not plain halving.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM
finding: Ablation lesson: entropy-only selection can pick questions whose answers are noisy (high marginal and high conditional entropy) and learn nothing; true gain subtracts the conditional entropy.
numbers: Entropy ablation and Split perform worse than full EIG in the paper's Fig. 2 and Table 1 (exact per-cell values not recorded here).
limits: Mechanism shown with a worked figure and ablations, not a field study.
agent_relevance: For tests with unreliable readings, the agent should not just choose the test that splits candidates evenly. Weight by test reliability.

source: Rouse (1987) Human Problem Solving in Complex Dynamic Environments (Georgia Tech project reports, includes Henneman's work)
finding: In a simulated communication-network failure-finding task, time to locate a failure varied with whether subjects used topographic, symptomatic or serendipitous search, and with how fast symptoms spread through the system.
numbers: Transfer-function models of average time to diagnosis explained more than 80% of variance; no consistent structure across subjects in the model terms.
limits: Only the progress-report text was read; the Henneman thesis behind it was not opened, and no per-strategy times are given in the report.
agent_relevance: Evidence that strategy mix matters but varies by person and event; do not assume one mode.

source: Morris & Rouse (1985) Review and evaluation of empirical research in troubleshooting (Human Factors 27:503-530)
finding: Reported (from a secondary summary only) as concluding that performance falls as complexity or time pressure rises, teaching theory does not make good troubleshooters, proceduralised strategy is the surest way to get a strategy used, and task knowledge matters more than aptitude.
numbers: Five conclusions listed; no numbers seen.
limits: Not opened; summary came from a search snippet. Treat as a lead to verify.
agent_relevance: If proceduralising is the dependable way to impose a strategy, that supports putting the strategy in the program, not the prompt.

source: Goldbeck, Bernstein, Hillix & Marx (1957) diagnostic behavior of electronic troubleshooting (as cited in searches)
finding: Not found. A search for this study returned nothing relevant, so no finding is recorded.
numbers: none
limits: Source not located; do not cite until verified.
agent_relevance: Open question for other angles: is there a controlled study that measured half-split efficiency in people?
